turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, October 30. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Alphabet lost roughly 12.6% of its value on Thursday, the worst single day in the company's history, and it was not because Google Cloud stopped growing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start with Iran, where a letter is doing the work that missiles have not. The New York Times reports Vice President Vance wrote to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, offering direct talks and saying he would lead the American delegation, delivered through Qatari mediators on October 25.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tehran's conditions, per Iranian state-linked media, are a regional ceasefire, unfreezing overseas assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US naval blockade. The IRGC-linked Tasnim says Tehran has the letter and has not replied.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the White House is sending two messages at once. The Wall Street Journal says the letter went out at Trump's direction, while Trump says he did not direct it, and that any decision on renewed strikes comes after the November 3 midterms.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So the diplomacy has an election-shaped deadline. Venues floated are Qatar or Turkey, possibly as soon as next week, but one Gulf outlet's claim of a signed memorandum has no second source, so treat it as noise.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ukraine now. A Russian strike on the Dnipro railway station on Thursday killed 14 people, with a jet-powered drone reported in the attack, and Zelensky put the day's toll at 19 across Dnipro, Kremenchuk and Chernihiv.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meanwhile the local truce around Oleshky in Kherson is holding. Russia has halted strikes there for aid access, and CNN credits Melania Trump with brokering it. Moscow's line is that the battlefield situation will determine when real talks begin, which is a polite way of saying not yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, the United States. The midterms are Tuesday, five days out. The Senate is 53 to 47 Republican, so Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kalshi has Democratic Senate control at about 65 to 67% as of Wednesday, a polling-model estimate sits closer to 58%, and the Silver Bulletin has Democrats as strong favorites for the House. CNN's own read is that the range of Senate outcomes is enormous.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A few state polls tell you why. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads by 7, and in Kansas, Democrat Hamilton is at 49 to Senator Marshall's 45. Leads in Texas, Ohio, Alaska and Maine sit inside normal polling error.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the point. A House takeover is the base case, and the Senate is a coin flip with a thumb on one side.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Iran file and the midterm file are linked on purpose. Trump has said the strike decision waits until after Tuesday, and a negotiated opening before the vote would be worth more to the White House than one after it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tehran can read a calendar too. Waiting five days costs it little, and a weaker White House after a bad night for Republicans would improve its bargaining position on exactly the sanctions and asset questions it listed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Back to Alphabet, because it's the cleanest example of the market's new rule. Third-quarter EPS was $2.12 against $3.02 expected, search ads were light, and free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion against an expected positive $2.7 billion.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And yet Google Cloud revenue was $30.7 billion, up about 103%, with $11.1 billion of operating income. The stock closed down about 12.6%, wiping out roughly $480 to $500 billion of market value, the second-largest one-day dollar loss in US market history.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Capex guidance for 2026 is unchanged at $195 to $205 billion, with a significant increase promised for 2027. Growth was never the question. The question is whether the cash comes back before the balance sheet runs out of patience.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Amazon reported after the bell. Revenue was $201.9 billion, up 12%, and EPS of $1.89 missed. AWS grew 39.3% to about $46 billion, the sixth straight quarter of acceleration, with a backlog of $578 billion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The catch is cash. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow is negative $42.4 billion, 2026 capex is about $220 billion, and the shares were down 6 to 7% in early trading.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Intel is the second shoe. Revenue was $16.5 billion, up 21%, and data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion, but the fourth-quarter guide of $15 to $16 billion came in far below the $17.05 billion Street number, and the stock is down sharply in early trading, somewhere from 16 to 25% depending on the hour.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A fab incident cost about 200 basis points of gross margin and management flagged PC weakness through at least the first half of 2027. It's the AI boom's old-economy tail.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One genuine winner. Eli Lilly posted adjusted EPS of $7.48 against roughly $6.26 expected, revenue of $24.4 billion, and raised its 2026 revenue guide to $91 to $92 billion from $85 to $87 billion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And a deal. DoorDash is buying Instacart for about $17 billion, $65 a share in cash and stock, roughly a 25% premium. Closing is not expected until late 2027 or early 2028, and an antitrust group is already urging regulators to block it, citing around 60% of third-party grocery delivery.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Seoul had the worst of it overnight. South Korea's KOSPI fell about 4.9% on Friday, with a sidecar halting program trading after KOSPI 200 futures dropped 5%, and chips led the slide.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tokyo followed, with the Nikkei off about 2%, and the Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in an 8 to 1 vote, with one board member dissenting in favor of a hike. The bank said underlying inflation is consistent with its 2% target, and that it will more than double its ETF sales from 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So Japan is telling you that it's normalizing slowly, while the Korean market is telling you what happens when the world's marginal chip dollar gets nervous. Hang Seng was up about 1.4% in the middle of all that.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Add crypto. Binance has suspended deposits, withdrawals and its Alpha trading after reports of a suspected hot-wallet hack. No loss figure yet, and Bitcoin is down about 3% to near $78,800.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At the United Nations on Wednesday, the General Assembly voted 130 to 17 with 25 abstentions to call for an end to the US embargo on Cuba. It's the 34th such vote, non-binding, and the lowest support since 1995. Last year it was 165 in favor.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: US Ambassador Waltz argued that major economies like Korea and Germany have shifted their positions, while Cuba accuses Washington of tariff and visa threats against supporters. The erosion is the story, because a symbolic vote only matters when the margin moves.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The tape is on the Markets tab. The argument is rotation. The Nasdaq fell 1.4% and the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%, but the Russell 2000 gained 1% to a 3-week high, and breadth was positive almost 2 to 1.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this wasn't a risk-off day, it was a quality-of-spend day. The money left the companies burning cash on compute and went to the ones that aren't, and the equal-weight S&P was up about 1.2%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The one number worth reading is the 10-year, at 4.99%, down 5.6 basis points and ending a 4-day rise. That came with a cooler Personal Consumption Expenditures print, headline 3.6%, core 3.1%, in line, and a GDP advance of 3.4% against 3.2% expected.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Strong growth, sticky inflation, and a Fed whose December hike is priced at around 80%. That mix is why a miss on free cash flow gets punished harder than a miss on earnings.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oil is the other pillar. Brent for January delivery closed at $110.80, with WTI near $102, and Brent popped after settlement on a report that Iran military options were briefed to the president. The Vance letter and the strike options are the same story told twice.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Friday's open is the test. Nasdaq futures are weaker, Amazon and Intel are both down, and Apple reports Monday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The watch item is whether the rotation holds when the mega-cap names are the ones falling. If small caps hold up with Alphabet, Amazon and Intel all down, that's a real regime change and not a one-day rebalance.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Deep dive today goes somewhere with no earnings call. On October 27, a team spanning the University of Washington, SLAC, Stanford and the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics announced the first dwarf planet candidate found in data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. It's called 2026 ED138.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: To be exact about what's claimed: it is a candidate, it is unconfirmed, and the size is an estimate. The reported range is 600 to 1,500 kilometers across, and that spread is the most interesting number in the story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why is the range so wide? We can't see a disk at that distance, can we?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No. At about 46 astronomical units, a bit farther than Pluto's average of roughly 40, it's a point of light. You know how bright it looks, you know how far away it is, so you can compute how much sunlight it reflects, but you can't separate size from reflectivity.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A small, shiny object and a large, dark one can look identical. If the surface is icy and bright, 600 kilometers is plenty. If it's dark, like much of the outer solar system's rubble, it has to be bigger to put out the same light. That assumed albedo is the whole 600 to 1,500 spread.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And infrared follow-up fixes it, because a body's heat glow depends on size in a different way than reflected light does.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly. Combine visible and infrared and you solve for both unknowns. For scale, Pluto is about 2,380 kilometers, Eris is about the same, and Ceres is about 940. So at the top of the range this is a Haumea or Makemake class world, and at the bottom it's something smaller than Ceres.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which brings in the definition, and the part everyone argues about. What actually makes something a dwarf planet?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The International Astronomical Union's 2006 rules. It orbits the Sun, it isn't a moon, and it has enough mass for its own gravity to pull it into a roughly round shape, called hydrostatic equilibrium. A full planet must also have cleared its orbital neighborhood. A dwarf planet hasn't.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the criterion is roundness, and nobody has photographed this thing well enough to see whether it's round.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right. In practice, astronomers estimate it. Rock is strong at small sizes and can hold a lumpy shape, ice gives way at a few hundred kilometers, so a body above roughly 400 to 600 kilometers of mostly ice is probably round. That's why the lower end of this range is borderline and the upper end is comfortable.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There are five officially recognized dwarf planets, Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake, and some outlets are calling this a possible sixth. Is that fair?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's fair as a headline and premature as a classification. The IAU doesn't have a fast process, and in practice the recognized list has barely changed since 2008. A lot of astronomers keep unofficial lists of dozens of likely candidates, so what's new here is less the object than how it was found.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And how was it found? Because that's the piece that matters for the observatory itself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Matthew Holman at the Center for Astrophysics led a search code built with Kevin Napier, and it ran on Rubin data from March to July of 2026. The orbit was then traced backward through archival images to 2016, which is how you get a stable orbit instead of a few weeks of dots.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So no dedicated telescope time. It's a software story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a software story on a data firehose. Rubin's survey is designed to image the whole southern sky repeatedly over 10 years. The telescope doesn't point at targets, it takes everything, so discoveries come from asking new questions of the same pile.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which flips how discovery works. The old model was a person with a hunch and a telescope, and the new model is a pipeline and a good linking algorithm.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And that matters for the population statistics. If one search found a body this big this far out, the open question is how many more sit in the archive. Distant objects move slowly, and linking detections across years is the hard part, so every improvement in the linking code pulls new bodies out of old data.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's a decent chance this isn't a one-off, then.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a decent chance we're about to get a census instead of a handful of celebrity objects. A census changes the science, because the shape of the distribution, how many bodies at each size and each orbit, tells you how the outer solar system formed and whether something big once shepherded it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the argument for not getting hung up on the label.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right. Calling it a planet or not is a negotiation, and the data is the real prize. If there turn out to be hundreds of round-ish icy worlds, the 2006 definition looks less like a settled line and more like a freeze-frame of what we could see.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One caution on the details. Some write-ups cite an orbital period and inclination that we couldn't verify, so we'll stick with what the research team stated: the size range, the distance, and the archival link back to 2016.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the honest status is a candidate with a measurable question. Infrared follow-up tells us whether it's 600 kilometers of bright ice or something Pluto-adjacent, and that single measurement decides which of the two headlines was right.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Energy, and the lens is deliverable megawatts, because this week's hyperscaler prints all say the same thing from different angles. Amazon's Andy Jassy said even at $220 billion of capex the company will not have enough capacity, and that blocks of hundreds of megawatts up to a gigawatt are being reserved well in advance.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Yet AWS's sequential dollar add actually slowed, from $4.65 billion to $3.75 billion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Management blamed uneven capacity landing, which is the tell. Demand isn't the constraint. AWS backlog is $578 billion, up $82 billion in a quarter. The revenue line is a proxy for energized capacity, and it moves when buildings get power, not when contracts get signed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Alphabet made the same point more bluntly. Its cloud backlog is about $561 billion, roughly 55% recognized within 24 months, and it began using third-party compute capacity at the end of the third quarter.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the new angle. Google is renting capacity from someone else because it couldn't build fast enough, and its Q3 capex of $51.4 billion was about 65% servers and networking, 35% data centers. The ratio matters, because servers are the part that depreciate on a 5-year clock, whether or not the shell has power.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Microsoft's version?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fiscal 2027 capex of roughly $170 billion, though sources disagree on whether that's fiscal or calendar, so check the filing. More than $50 billion in the December quarter, and the CFO blamed third-party GPU provider delays for part of the undershoot, pushing some capacity into the first half of 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the delivery risk list now includes your neocloud counterparty, not just turbines and transformers.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly. Add the chain: you sign a lease, a developer needs interconnection, a utility needs equipment, a chip vendor needs to ship, and a neocloud has to land the racks. Any one late link strands the other four.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that change how you read the capex guides?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It changes which line you trust. A capex number tells you what was ordered. The delivered-capacity number, the megawatts energized, is what drives revenue, and none of the three companies disclosed it this quarter. Until that appears, sequential cloud revenue is the best public gauge of what actually got plugged in.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the free cash flow hit comes from paying for equipment months before it earns anything.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the timing mismatch in Amazon's trailing figure. Property and equipment purchases rose $94.8 billion year over year, while the revenue those purchases support arrives only as buildings energize. The gap between the two is the negative free cash flow investors just priced.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the supply side, the Department of Energy announced a conditional commitment of up to $5 billion in loans to Constellation for uprates at 8 plants: Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, Quad Cities, Calvert Cliffs and Limerick.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It adds roughly 1.1 gigawatts, about one large reactor's worth, but per-site megawatts and schedule weren't disclosed, and it's conditional on due diligence. Constellation says it has already committed more than $7 billion for 1,080 megawatts delivering to Google, Amazon and Meta.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which means the power is largely pre-sold.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So the federal loan lowers the cost of capital on megawatts that already have buyers. It accelerates delivery, but it doesn't create supply beyond the uprate itself, and that's a useful distinction when you hear it described as a new reactor.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Texas is filtering the other end of the queue.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A Public Utility Commission rule requires $50,000 per megawatt of requested peak demand as financial security, effective October 8, per a law-firm summary, so confirm against the rule text. At that price a 1 gigawatt request posts $50 million.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Queue size estimates range from about 226 gigawatts to 474, depending on the date and the definition.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is why a per-megawatt deposit is the right tool. It doesn't shrink the queue by decree, it reprices optionality, and the speculative requests are the first to fall away. Modo Energy tracks around 92 gigawatts of advanced data-center load in ERCOT, and that's the number to hold against the headline queue.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the takeaway for a developer?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Capacity is sold out, the utility and the chip vendor set the clock, and credit is moving from the speculative to the committed. The winners are the ones with a signed utility agreement and a delivered shell, not the biggest queue position.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does a company like Amazon need to worry about the queue deposit?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Not at that scale, because it has balance-sheet-backed utility agreements. The deposit bites the mid-sized developer who stacked ten speculative requests hoping one clears. At $50,000 per megawatt, ten 500 megawatt requests cost $250 million to hold, and that is a very different carrying cost than a free option.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So expect fewer, firmer requests.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And a cleaner signal for utilities about which load will really show up, which is what ratebase planning has been missing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ngayong umaga, dalawang salita na kapwa ginagamit sa balita tungkol sa ekonomiya. Ang una ay "umaray."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "umaray" ay literal na mapasigaw o mapadaing dahil sa sakit, pero sa balita ay ginagamit para sa mga taong tumututol sa mabigat na gastos. Halimbawa, umaray ang mga mamimili sa presyo ng gasolina at bigas.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Mas matalinghaga ito kaysa "nagreklamo." Kapag sinabing "umaray," ramdam mo na masakit na sa bulsa, hindi lang basta may reklamo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama. At madalas itong ginagamit sa headline, dahil maikli at may tindi. Sa pang-araw-araw na usapan, puwede mo ring sabihing "Umaray ako sa bayarin ngayong buwan."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ngayon ang pangalawa, "pagtugon." Ito ang pagsagot sa isang problema sa pamamagitan ng aksyon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pormal ito at madalas mong maririnig sa mga pahayag ng pamahalaan. Kailangan ng mabilis na pagtugon ng gobyerno sa paghina ng piso.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magkaiba ito sa "sagot." Ang "sagot" ay karaniwang tumutukoy sa tanong, samantalang ang "pagtugon" ay gawa o hakbang para ayusin ang suliranin.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kaya may "pagtugon sa sakuna," "pagtugon sa krisis," at "pagtugon sa pangangailangan ng mamamayan." Laging may kasamang obligasyon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pansinin ang ugnayan ng dalawa. Kapag umaray ang taumbayan, inaasahan ang pagtugon ng pamahalaan. Isa itong hugis ng usapan sa balita ngayong linggo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tatandaan natin: umaray, ang pag-daing sa mabigat na gastos, at pagtugon, ang aksyon sa problema. Pakinggan natin pareho sa susunod na bahagi.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Umaray ang mga Pilipino sa pagbagsak ng piso, na umabot sa P64.17 kada dolyar noong Martes, ang ikaanim na magkakasunod na record low.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Inaasahan ang mabilis na pagtugon ng Bangko Sentral at ng pamahalaan, ngunit sinabi ni Pangulong Marcos noong Miyerkoles na huwag mag-panic at na nasa labas ng kontrol ng patakaran ang presyo ng langis na nagtutulak sa implasyon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bumawi nang bahagya ang piso sa P64.025 noong Miyerkoles at P63.85 noong Huwebes, ayon sa Bankers Association of the Philippines.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English: the market isn't buying a quick fix. Cuisia has said 65 is within reach, and BPI's downside case is 66.40 by year-end. The peso's link to oil is the story, and Brent at $110 is the tailwind for the dollar.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Philippines imports nearly all its oil, so the peso and inflation are the same problem. That's why the president's line that oil is beyond policy control is both honest and politically uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the budget, Senate President Gatchalian warned that a reenacted 2027 budget would further weaken the economy, and is pushing to pass the P7.2 trillion budget on time. He floated cutting travel and seminar spending as a way to find savings.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The House says it won't recall its bill, so the Senate plans to correct the budget without a recall. Plenary debates are expected to start in November, and a P50 billion military modernization lump sum is already drawing attention given the Supreme Court's earlier ruling on lump sums.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last item, the Duterte trial. The International Criminal Court recognized 96 alleged victims to participate in the proceedings, though participation status isn't final. The trial opens on November 30, on three counts of crimes against humanity.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which means the ICC calendar and the Senate budget calendar now collide in December. A reenacted budget, a trial and a record-low peso is a lot of simultaneous pressure on a single administration.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more thread on the peso. Remittances and the oil bill pull in opposite directions, and with oil at these levels the import side is winning.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The number to watch is the October inflation print, due in the coming days. If it follows the oil price, the central bank's next move becomes the next big story, and the government's line that oil is beyond control will be tested by households, not economists.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both from the currency story. The first is 升值, shēngzhí, to appreciate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 升值 is used for currencies and assets that gain value against something else. 人民币升值了，出口企业的压力就更大。(When the renminbi appreciates, the pressure on exporters grows.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And it's different from 上涨, which just means a price goes up. 升值 implies value gained in relative terms, so you wouldn't say a loaf of bread 升值.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, the opposite is 贬值, depreciate, and common collocations are 人民币升值, 房产升值, and 升值预期, the expectation of appreciation. It's neutral-to-formal, fine in speech and in the news.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word, a pattern: 对……造成冲击, to have a shock impact on something.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a written, formal collocation. 美元走强对新兴市场造成冲击。(A stronger dollar has a shock impact on emerging markets.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How is that different from 影响, which also means affect?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 影响 is neutral and covers everything. 冲击 stresses a sudden, disruptive blow, like a wave hitting. You'd use 对出口造成冲击 for a sharp shock to exports, and 影响出口 for a general influence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Handy for the news, because markets, the economy and exports are the usual objects after 对. This second one is the abstract collocation to watch for in the China segment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So 升值 for the yuan gaining, and 对……造成冲击 for a blow to something. Both come up in a minute.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管美元走强，人民币依然升值，在岸价一度触及6.6620，创四年来新高。(Even as the dollar strengthened, the yuan still appreciated, with the onshore rate touching 6.6620, a four-year high.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Note the other half. The central bank set its daily midpoint at 6.7147 per dollar, weaker than the 6.6596 that models expected, which reads as leaning against too-fast appreciation. That's a single-source figure, so treat it as indicative.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 升值太快会对出口企业造成冲击。(Appreciating too fast would have a shock impact on exporters.) The CFETS basket index is at 103.75, its highest since July 2022, which means the strength is broad and not only against the dollar.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is the two-speed story in one chart. A strong currency is a signal of confidence, but a stronger yuan also squeezes the export sector that is carrying growth, and Beijing is trying to hold the line in between.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Data to watch is tomorrow's official manufacturing PMI. September was 50.1, up from 49.8 in August, and a reading under 50 with a firmer yuan would be an uncomfortable combination.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the next political date is APEC on November 18, with Trump saying a meeting with Xi is scheduled.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The trade truce is the background. Reports say the rare earth and tariff pause was extended into January 2027, though sources conflict on the exact date, and Treasury Secretary Bessent has cited shortfalls in Chinese farm purchases and rare earth shipments.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the yuan's strength is partly a bet on a deal. If APEC disappoints, the strength becomes a vulnerability.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Art first. Christie's holds its first-ever Abu Dhabi fine art sale on Sunday, November 1, titled MAWASIM, twenty years of modern and contemporary Middle Eastern art, about 70 lots with a total estimate of around $130 million.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The headline lot is Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken from 1923, estimated at $60 to $80 million. It's being shown in Abu Dhabi alongside a Rothko and a Picasso, then goes to the New York sale on November 17. That's a Bauhaus-period Kandinsky, geometric, post-Russia, built from sharp angles, and it's the kind of picture that can carry a sale on its own.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is the Gulf making a case as a market, not just a buyer.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Christie's CEO told The National that Abu Dhabi is gaining ground, and Sotheby's debuts its own Abu Dhabi sale on December 10, with a Monet still life and a late Warhol screenprint. Two houses in the same market in six weeks is a bet that the buyer base is now local enough to hold an auction.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Different register, same theme of place. In Los Angeles, the Museum of Contemporary Art opens Cecilia Vicuña's The Dream of Water: Quipu of Encounters Maricunga, running November 15 to June 6, 2027.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's one of two inaugural shows for the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Environment and Art Prize, $100,000 each, the other going to Julian Charrière. Vicuña's subject is the Maricunga salt flats in the Atacama, where lithium extraction and water collide, and she builds with a quipu, the Andean knotted-cord record, assembled with local artists, young people, scientists and Indigenous water defenders.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: It hasn't opened, so there are no reviews, but the connection is striking. Lithium for batteries is the physical side of the energy story we just did.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the form is the argument. A quipu is a way of keeping accounts without writing, and the piece ends with a ritual quipu assembly. The question the show poses is who keeps the ledger on water.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Op-eds. In the Washington Post on Wednesday, the political analyst Ruy Teixeira of the American Enterprise Institute argued that a blue wave could ultimately cripple the Democratic Party.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The steelman: Democrats are near-certain to retake the House and favored in the Senate, Trump is unpopular and cost of living is a drag. But a win hides the party's weak standing with working-class voters, much as a decent 2022 midterm fed the belief that Biden was viable. Success breeds complacency heading into 2028.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter-take is that this reads as a pre-emptive concession of victory, and Teixeira has made a nearly identical fool's-gold argument before, so the thesis doesn't depend on the evidence. A midterm win funds oversight, state power and candidate recruitment, which are real assets.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the polling points the other way. Gallup finds voters rank the economy, healthcare and Iran highest, and those are issues moving toward Democrats, not away.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So the strongest version isn't don't win, it's don't mistake winning for a coalition. Whether the class-realignment story is right is something the exit polls will test on Tuesday more than any column can.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Michael Barone's syndicated column is the mirror image, noting that with under two weeks to go things look bad for Trump's Republicans. His own caveat is the useful one: polls and midterm trends have misled before.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is a fair note for a show that just read you Kalshi odds.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One Good Thing. Marilyn Hampton is 76 and spent 39 years as a custodian in the Aubrey school district, north of Dallas. She bought supplies for kids who needed them, helped students prepare for tests, and worked the football gates.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: She retired in 2022 and still works with infants at the district's early learning center. She has only a high school education and has long felt she failed by not going to college.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This week the school board asked her to roll out a red carpet, and under it was the name of the district's new elementary school: Marilyn Hampton Elementary. It opens next August.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: She cried and said, "I can't speak."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Friday, October 30. Have a good weekend, and we'll see you Monday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Thanks for listening.
